# 3.2 Units of Measurement

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

All metric units are based on multiples of 10, which is what makes converting between them a matter of moving a decimal point rather than remembering an awkward factor. The system is built from a small set of base units, with prefixes doing the work of scaling them up and down.

## The seven SI base units

The **International System of Units (SI)** defines seven base quantities. Every other unit in chemistry is assembled from these.

| Physical quantity | Unit | Symbol |
|---|---|---|
| Mass | kilogram | kg |
| Length | metre | m |
| Time | second | s |
| Temperature | kelvin | K |
| Amount of substance | mole | mol |
| Electric current | ampere | A |
| Luminous intensity | candela | cd |

## Common prefixes

A prefix multiplies the base unit by a power of ten. Learning the factor is more useful than learning the name, because the factor is what goes into a conversion.

| Prefix | Symbol | Factor |
|---|---|---|
| Mega | M | $10^{6}$ |
| Kilo | k | $10^{3}$ |
| Deci | d | $10^{-1}$ |
| Centi | c | $10^{-2}$ |
| Milli | m | $10^{-3}$ |
| Micro | $\mu$ | $10^{-6}$ |
| Nano | n | $10^{-9}$ |
| Pico | p | $10^{-12}$ |

## Volume

Volume is a derived quantity — it is a length cubed — so the metric volume units line up exactly with the metric length units:

$$1\ \mathrm{L} = 1\ \mathrm{dm^{3}} \qquad 1\ \mathrm{mL} = 1\ \mathrm{cm^{3}} \qquad 1\ \mathrm{L} = 1000\ \mathrm{mL}$$

The second of these is the one used most often in the laboratory: a millilitre and a cubic centimetre are the same volume under two names.

## Mass and weight

One gram is defined as the mass of $1\ \mathrm{cm^{3}}$ of water at 4 degrees Celsius. Mass and weight are not the same thing — weight is the force gravity exerts on a mass:

$$W = m \cdot g$$

## Energy

**Energy** is the capacity to do work or to produce heat. Its SI unit is the **joule**; the common non-SI unit is the **calorie**. The two are related by

$$1\ \mathrm{J} = 0.2390\ \text{calorie}$$

## Temperature

**Temperature** is a measure of how hot or cold an object is. Two scales are used: Celsius and Kelvin. They are the same size of degree, offset from one another, so converting is a matter of adding or subtracting:

$$K = {}^{\circ}\mathrm{C} + 273 \qquad {}^{\circ}\mathrm{C} = K - 273$$

The zero point on the Kelvin scale, **absolute zero**, is equal to $-273.15\ {}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ — so where more accuracy is wanted, use 273.15 rather than 273 in the conversions above.

## Density

**Density** is the ratio of the mass of an object to its volume:

$$\text{density} = \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}$$

Its SI unit is $\mathrm{kg/m^{3}}$, following directly from the base units for mass and length.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Energy** | The capacity to do work or to produce heat |
| **Joule** | The SI unit of energy; $1\ \mathrm{J} = 0.2390$ calorie |
| **Temperature** | A measure of how hot or cold an object is |
| **Absolute zero** | The zero point on the Kelvin scale, equal to $-273.15\ {}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ |
| **Density** | The ratio of the mass of an object to its volume; SI unit $\mathrm{kg/m^{3}}$ |

# 3.3 Solving Conversion Problems

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Conversion factors

A **conversion factor** is a ratio of equivalent measurements. Because the top and bottom of the ratio describe the same physical quantity in two different units, multiplying by a conversion factor changes the units without changing the quantity.

The pattern to watch for is that the two halves always run in opposite directions:

- smaller number with the larger unit,
- larger number with the smaller unit.

So $1\ \mathrm{m}$ pairs with $100\ \mathrm{cm}$: the same length, expressed as a small count of large units or a large count of small ones.

Conversion factors are defined or exact quantities, not measured ones. That is why they carry an **unlimited number of significant figures** and never limit the precision of an answer — only the measured values in a calculation do that.

## Dimensional analysis

**Dimensional analysis** is a way to analyse and solve problems using the units of the measurement. You chain conversion factors together so that the unwanted units cancel and only the wanted unit is left standing. If the units come out right, the arrangement of the numbers was right too.

Expressing 750 nanometres in metres:

$$750\ \mathrm{nm} \times \frac{1\ \mathrm{m}}{10^{9}\ \mathrm{nm}} = 7.50 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$$

The conversion factor was deliberately written with nanometres on the bottom so that the $\mathrm{nm}$ in the starting measurement cancels against it, leaving metres. Had it been written the other way up, the units would have come out as $\mathrm{nm^{2}/m}$ — a signal that the factor needed inverting.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Conversion factor** | A ratio of equivalent measurements; a defined or exact quantity with an unlimited number of significant figures |
| **Dimensional analysis** | A way to analyse and solve problems using the units of the measurement |

# 5.1 Revising the Atomic Model

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The Bohr model

In the **Bohr model**, electrons move in certain circular orbits with allowed energy states around the nucleus. Each orbit is designated by a **quantum number** $n$, taking the values $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ The important word is *allowed*: an electron cannot sit at any energy it likes, only at the particular energies the model permits.

## De Broglie and the wave nature of matter

Louis de Broglie proposed that particles of matter should behave like waves and exhibit a wavelength, just as waves of light behave like particles of matter. The symmetry is the point — if light, long treated as a wave, can act as a particle, then matter, long treated as particles, can act as a wave.

## The Heisenberg uncertainty principle

The **Heisenberg uncertainty principle** states that the position and the velocity of a moving object cannot be measured and known at the same time. This is what forces the abandonment of definite orbits: if an electron's position and velocity cannot both be pinned down, a fixed path around the nucleus cannot be drawn.

## The quantum mechanical model

The **quantum mechanical model** determines the allowed energies an electron can have and the probability of finding the electron in various locations around the nucleus of an atom. It replaces a definite path with a distribution of likelihood.

An **atomic orbital** is represented pictorially as a region of space in which there is a high probability of finding an electron. It is a probability map, not a track.

## Atomic orbitals and how many there are

Atomic orbitals are represented by the letters **s, p, d and f**, and these are also called **sublevels**.

The counting rules build on one another:

- Each principal energy level $n$ has $n$ sublevels — the principal quantum number always equals the number of sublevels within that principal energy level.
- Each type of sublevel holds a different number of orbitals: s has 1, p has 3, d has 5, f has 7.
- Each energy level $n$ therefore consists of $n^{2}$ orbitals in total.
- A maximum of two electrons can occupy an orbital.
- Putting the last two together, the maximum number of electrons in a principal energy level is $2n^{2}$.

| $n$ | Sublevels present | Orbitals ($n^{2}$) | Maximum electrons ($2n^{2}$) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | s | 1 | 2 |
| 2 | s, p | 4 | 8 |
| 3 | s, p, d | 9 | 18 |
| 4 | s, p, d, f | 16 | 32 |

Every entry in the last column is just twice the one before it in the third, because the two-electrons-per-orbital limit is the only thing linking them.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Bohr model** | A model in which electrons move in certain circular orbits with allowed energy states around the nucleus, each designated by a quantum number $n$ |
| **Heisenberg uncertainty principle** | The position and velocity of a moving object cannot be measured and known at the same time |
| **Quantum mechanical model** | A model that determines the allowed energies an electron can have and the probability of finding the electron in various locations around the nucleus |
| **Atomic orbital** | A region of space in which there is a high probability of finding an electron |
| **Sublevel** | One of the s, p, d and f divisions of a principal energy level; level $n$ has $n$ sublevels |

# 5.2 Electron Arrangement in Atoms

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Electron configurations** are the ways in which electrons are arranged in various orbitals around the nuclei of atoms. They matter because they determine the chemical properties of the elements and are the origin of the periodic trends — the arrangement of the electrons is what the rest of chemistry is built on. The configuration written for an element is normally the most stable arrangement of its electrons, which is the **ground state** of the atom.

Four rules govern how the electrons are placed.

## I. The Aufbau principle

**Electrons occupy the orbitals of lowest energy first.** Filling proceeds up the energy ranking, so an orbital is only used once everything below it has been dealt with.

## II. The Pauli exclusion principle

**An atomic orbital may describe at most two electrons, and they must have opposite spins.** **Spin** is a quantum mechanical property of electrons that may be thought of as clockwise or counterclockwise.

Two electrons of opposite spin occupying one orbital are said to be **paired**; a single electron alone in an orbital is **unpaired**.

## III. Hund's rule

**Electrons occupy orbitals of the same energy in a way that makes the number of electrons with the same spin direction as large as possible.** Where three orbitals of equal energy are available, three electrons take one orbital each rather than doubling up in one of them.

## IV. Condensed electron configurations

Writing out every electron becomes unwieldy for heavier atoms, so the inner shell is abbreviated. In a **condensed electron configuration**, the electron configuration of the nearest noble-gas element of lower atomic number — that is, the last element of each horizontal period — is represented by its chemical symbol in brackets.

Noble gases are used for this because they are the most stable elements: helium (He), neon (Ne), argon (Ar), krypton (Kr).

## Ground state and excited state

The ground state is the most stable, lowest energy state of the atom. If an electron is promoted into a higher orbital the atom is in an **excited state**.

| State | Configuration of carbon |
|---|---|
| Ground state | $1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{2}$ |
| Excited state | $1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{1}\,3s^{1}$ |

Both describe six electrons; the excited state simply has one of them sitting higher than it needs to.

## Exceptional electron configurations

Some actual electron configurations differ from those assigned using the Aufbau principle. The two to know are chromium and copper:

| Element | Actual configuration |
|---|---|
| Chromium | $1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{6}\,3s^{2}\,3p^{6}\,3d^{5}\,4s^{1}$ |
| Copper | $1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{6}\,3s^{2}\,3p^{6}\,3d^{10}\,4s^{1}$ |

The reason is stability. Although half-filled sublevels are not as stable as filled sublevels, they are more stable than other configurations — so chromium takes a half-filled $3d^{5}$ and copper a filled $3d^{10}$, each at the cost of leaving only one electron in the $4s$ orbital.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|

# 6.1 Organizing the Elements

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## I. Searching for an organizing principle

As chemists began to use scientific methods to search for elements, the rate of discovery increased. In the single decade from 1765 to 1775, chemists discovered five new elements, and in the 1790s Lavoisier drew up a list of 23 elements. A growing list needs an organising principle, and the early chemists used the properties of the elements to sort them into groups.

Two early schemes tried to find the repeating pattern:

- The **law of triads** grouped the elements in threes; the elements in a triad have similar chemical properties.
- The **law of octaves** grouped them in eights: when the elements were arranged in order of increasing atomic mass, the properties repeated every eighth element.

## II. Mendeleev's periodic table

Mendeleev arranged the elements in his periodic table in order of increasing atomic mass, placing elements with similar properties in the same row. Where the pattern demanded an element that nobody had yet found, he left a gap — and predicted that an element would be discovered to fill each space, along with what its properties would be, based on its location in the table.

## III. Today's periodic table

The **periodic law** states that when elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number, there is a periodic repetition of their physical and chemical properties.

The shift from mass to atomic number came from H. G. J. Moseley, who determined an atomic number for each known element. The modern periodic table arranges elements in order of increasing atomic number, in **7 rows (periods)** and **18 groups (families)**.

This is the sharpest point in the section: Mendeleev found the correct pattern even though he arranged the elements according to the wrong property. His table worked because atomic masses generally increase along with atomic number, so ordering by mass usually produces the same sequence as ordering by atomic number. Element number 101 is named after Mendeleev in recognition of his contribution to chemistry.

## IV. Metals, nonmetals and metalloids

Two directional statements cover the broad classification:

- Across a period, the properties of elements become less metallic and more nonmetallic.
- Down a group, the properties of elements become less nonmetallic and more metallic.

### Metals

- **Lustre**, or shine, which is caused by the metal's ability to reflect light.
- Good conductors of heat and electricity. Copper is second only to silver as a conductor of electric current.
- Solid at room temperature, with the exception of mercury.
- **Malleable** — can be hammered into thin sheets without breaking. Aluminium is one of the metals that can be shaped into a thin sheet, or foil.
- **Ductile** — can be drawn into wires.

### Nonmetals

There is a greater variation in physical properties among the nonmetals than among the metals, so the description has to be given as a range rather than a rule:

- Most are gases at room temperature, including nitrogen and oxygen.
- A few are solids, such as sulfur and phosphorus.
- Bromine is a dark-red liquid.
- Usually gases or brittle solids; the solids are dull in appearance.
- Poor conductors of heat and electricity, with graphite as an exception.

### Semimetals (metalloids)

- Slight lustre.
- Conduct electricity at high temperature.
- Brittle.
- Their behaviour can often be controlled by changing the conditions — which is exactly what makes them useful.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Law of triads** | An early grouping of elements in threes; the elements in a triad have similar chemical properties |
| **Law of octaves** | An early grouping in eights: arranged in order of increasing atomic mass, the properties repeat every eighth element |
| **Periodic law** | When elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number, there is a periodic repetition of their physical and chemical properties |
| **Period** | One of the 7 rows of the periodic table |
| **Group (family)** | One of the 18 columns of the periodic table |
| **Lustre** | The shine of a metal, caused by its ability to reflect light |
| **Malleable** | Able to be hammered into thin sheets without breaking |
| **Ductile** | Able to be drawn into wires |
| **Semimetal (metalloid)** | An element with slight lustre that is brittle and conducts electricity at high temperature |

# 6.2 Classifying the Elements

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## I. Reading the periodic table

The periods are not all the same length, because the number of orbitals available grows as you go down the table:

| Periods | Length |
|---|---|
| Periods 1–3 | Shorter periods — 2, 8, 8 elements |
| Periods 4–5 | Longer periods — 18, 18 elements |
| Periods 6–7 | 32 elements |

In total there are now 7 periods and 18 groups.

The **International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC)** is the organisation that sets standards for chemistry. It has its own numbering scheme for the groups, which has not been widely adopted.

## II. Electron configurations in groups

The electrons that occupy the highest principal energy level are the atom's outermost electrons. These are the **valence electrons** — the ones involved in chemical bonding, and therefore the ones largely responsible for an atom's chemical behaviour. For lighter elements, those with atomic number below 30, all the outermost electrons are valence electrons.

The periodic table is structured so that elements with the same pattern of outermost-level electron configuration are arranged in columns. That structure is what makes a group a group: elements in a column behave alike because their outer electrons are arranged alike.

### The four blocks

The table divides into four sections — the s, p, d and f blocks.

| Block | Width | Elements it contains | Classification |
|---|---|---|---|
| s | 2 columns | Hydrogen, helium, Group 1A and Group 2A | Representative elements |
| p | 6 columns | Group 3A to Group 8A (except He) | Representative elements |
| d | 10 columns | Group 1B to Group 8B (groups 3–12) | Transition elements |
| f | 14 columns | Lanthanide series, actinide series | Inner transition elements |

**Representative elements** are the s-block and p-block elements taken together. Most are solids, a few are gases at room temperature, and bromine is the only liquid among them. For these elements the group number equals the number of electrons in the highest occupied energy level — which is why the group number is such a quick route to the valence electron count.

### Classifying by the highest occupied energy level

The blocks can also be defined directly from the electron configuration, which is the more fundamental statement of the same classification:

| Class | Condition | Configuration range |
|---|---|---|
| Representative elements | Only the s or p sublevel is partially filled | $ns^{1}$–$ns^{2}$, $ns^{2}np^{1}$–$ns^{2}np^{6}$ |
| Transition metals | The s sublevel and the nearby d sublevel contain electrons | $(n-1)d^{1}ns^{2}$–$(n-1)d^{10}ns^{2}$ |
| Inner transition metals | The s sublevel and the nearby f sublevel contain electrons | $(n-2)f^{1}ns^{2}$–$(n-2)f^{14}ns^{2}$ |

Note where the sublevel being filled sits relative to the outermost level: for the transition metals it is one level down, $(n-1)$, and for the inner transition metals two levels down, $(n-2)$.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **IUPAC** | The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, the organisation that sets standards for chemistry |
| **Valence electrons** | The electrons that occupy the highest principal energy level; the electrons involved in chemical bonding |
| **Representative elements** | The 2-column s-block and 6-column p-block elements, whose group number equals the number of electrons in the highest occupied energy level |
| **Transition elements** | The 10-column d-block elements, in which the s sublevel and the nearby d sublevel contain electrons |
| **Inner transition elements** | The 14-column f-block elements — the lanthanide and actinide series — in which the s sublevel and the nearby f sublevel contain electrons |

# 6.3 Periodic Trends

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Many properties of the elements change in a predictable way as you move through the periodic table, and these systematic variations are called **periodic trends**. Almost every trend here is explained by the same single idea — the attraction force between the electrons and the nucleus — so it is worth tracking that quantity rather than memorising four separate lists.

## I. Trends in atomic size

The **atomic radius** is one-half of the distance between the nuclei of two atoms of the same element when the atoms are joined. It is often measured in picometres (pm).

**Trend 1: atoms get larger going down a group.** Going down a group adds more energy levels, so the attraction decreases, the outermost electrons sit further out, and the size increases. Along group 1, then, $\mathrm{Li} < \mathrm{Na} < \mathrm{K}$.

**Trend 2: atoms get smaller moving from left to right across each period.** Moving across a period keeps the electrons in the same energy level but adds more protons, so the attraction increases, the outermost electrons are pulled closer, and the atom size decreases. Along period 3, then, $\mathrm{Na} > \mathrm{Mg} > \mathrm{Al}$.

## II. Trends in ionic size

An **ion** is an atom or group of atoms that has a positive or negative charge. An ion with a positive charge is a **cation** — metals lose electrons easily — and an ion with a negative charge is an **anion** — nonmetals gain electrons easily.

The **octet rule** explains why: atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons in order to acquire a full set of valence electrons. For most energy levels a full set is 8 valence electrons — 2 in the s orbital and 6 in the p orbitals — with an exception for the first energy level, which is full with only 2 electrons. So the elements on the right-hand side of the periodic table tend to gain electrons and become anions, the elements on the left-hand side tend to lose electrons and become cations, and in both cases the outcome is a complete set of valence electrons and a stable arrangement. Noble gases already have one, so they neither gain nor lose electrons.

Forming an ion changes the size, and the reason given is the repulsion between the electrons themselves:

- **Positive ions become smaller.** Losing electrons reduces the repulsion between the remaining electrons, so the radius of a cation is smaller than that of the atom: $\mathrm{Na^{+}} < \mathrm{Na}$.
- **Negative ions become larger.** Gaining electrons increases the repulsion between the electrons, so the radius of an anion is larger than that of the atom: $\mathrm{Cl^{-}} > \mathrm{Cl}$.

Three trends follow:

**Trend 1: ions get larger going down a group.**

**Trend 2: ions get smaller from left to right.** The anions in one period and the cations of the next period have the same number of electrons, but the proton number in the nucleus keeps increasing, so the attraction force increases and the ion size decreases.

**Trend 3: for the same element, the species with fewer electrons — more positive or less negative — is the smaller one.**

## III. Trends in ionisation energy

An atom's **ionisation energy** ($I$) is the energy needed to remove one of its electrons. Atoms with a high $I$ hold onto their electrons tightly; atoms with a low $I$ are more likely to lose their outermost electrons.

**Trend 1: ionisation energy decreases as you move down a group**, because there are more energy levels and the outer electrons are further from the nucleus.

**Trend 2: ionisation energy increases as you move from left to right across a period**, because the atoms get smaller, so the outer electrons are nearer to the nucleus and more energy is required to remove them.

These are exactly the opposite of the trends for atomic radius, and that is not a coincidence: radius is inversely proportional to the attraction, while ionisation energy is proportional to it. One quantity, read two ways.

**Successive ionisation energies** are the energies required to remove electrons beyond the first.

**Trend 3: the ionisation energy increases for every electron removed.** There is more to it than a steady rise, though — an atom holds the electrons in its noble gas inner core much more strongly than it holds its valence electrons, so there is a large jump in the sequence at the point where the atom begins to lose an inner electron.

## IV. Trends in electronegativity

**Electronegativity (EN)** is the ability of an atom of an element to attract electrons when the atom is in a compound.

Electronegativity values have no units. They are neither an energy nor a property that can be directly measured — which sets electronegativity apart from atomic radius and ionisation energy, both of which are measurable quantities.

The comparison to hold onto is that nonmetals have higher electronegativity than metals.

## Summary of the trends

| Property | Down a group | Across a period (left to right) |
|---|---|---|
| Atomic radius | Increases | Decreases |
| Ionic radius | Increases | Decreases |
| Ionisation energy | Decreases | Increases |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Periodic trends** | The systematic, predictable variations in the properties of the elements as you move through the periodic table |
| **Atomic radius** | One-half of the distance between the nuclei of two atoms of the same element when the atoms are joined |
| **Ion** | An atom or group of atoms that has a positive or negative charge |
| **Cation** | An ion with a positive charge |
| **Anion** | An ion with a negative charge |
| **Octet rule** | Atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons in order to acquire a full set of valence electrons |
| **Ionisation energy ($I$)** | The energy needed to remove one of an atom's electrons |
| **Successive ionisation energies** | The energies required to remove electrons beyond the first electron |
| **Electronegativity (EN)** | The ability of an atom of an element to attract electrons when the atom is in a compound |

# 7.1 Ions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The forces that link atoms together to form the different kinds of matter are called **chemical bonds**. Which bond forms, and between which atoms, is decided almost entirely by the outermost electrons — so that is where the chapter starts.

## I. Valence electrons

**Valence electrons** are the electrons in the highest occupied energy level of an element's atoms.

To find the number of valence electrons in an atom of a representative element, simply look at its group number: Group 1A elements have 1 valence electron, Group 7A elements have 7. The exception to watch for is helium, which has two valence electrons, while the other noble gases have eight.

**Electron dot structures** are diagrams that show the valence electrons in the atoms of an element as dots. Because the count follows the group number, all the elements within a given group have the same number of electron dots in their structures — helium again being the exception. These diagrams are what will be used to show how chemical bonds form in a chemical reaction.

## II. The octet rule

Noble gases such as neon and argon are non-reactive in chemical reactions. Atoms of each of the noble gases, except helium, have eight electrons in their highest occupied energy levels, giving the general electron configuration $ns^{2}np^{6}$. Non-reactivity and a full outer level go together, and the octet rule generalises that observation.

**The octet rule states that in forming compounds, atoms tend to achieve the electron configuration of a noble gas.** Two routes lead there:

- Atoms of metals tend to lose their valence electrons, which leaves a complete octet in the next-lowest energy level.
- Atoms of some nonmetals tend to gain electrons, or to share electrons with another nonmetal atom or atoms, to achieve a complete octet.

The octet rule applies to atoms in most compounds — "most", not all, so expect exceptions later.

## III. Formation of ions

An **ion** is an atom that is no longer neutral because it has lost or gained electrons.

- A positively charged ion, or **cation**, is produced when an atom loses one or more valence electrons.
- A negatively charged ion, or **anion**, is produced when an atom gains one or more valence electrons.

### Naming ions

| Type | Rule | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Cation | The element name, unchanged | $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ = sodium ion |
| Anion | The stem of the element name, ending in *-ide* | $\mathrm{Cl^{-}}$ = chloride ion |

The ions produced when atoms of chlorine and the other halogens gain electrons are called **halide ions**.

### Transition metal cations

The charges of the cations of the transition metals may vary. This is why a transition metal in a compound cannot be named from its symbol alone — the charge has to be specified.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Chemical bonds** | The forces that link atoms together to form the different kinds of matter |
| **Valence electrons** | The electrons in the highest occupied energy level of an element's atoms |
| **Electron dot structure** | A diagram that shows the valence electrons in the atoms of an element as dots |
| **Octet rule** | In forming compounds, atoms tend to achieve the electron configuration of a noble gas |
| **Ion** | An atom that is no longer neutral because it has lost or gained electrons |
| **Cation** | A positively charged ion, produced when an atom loses one or more valence electrons |
| **Anion** | A negatively charged ion, produced when an atom gains one or more valence electrons |
| **Halide ion** | The ion produced when an atom of chlorine or another halogen gains an electron |

# 7.2 Ionic Bonds and Ionic Compounds

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Formation of ionic compounds

An **ionic compound** is a compound composed of cations and anions. Although they are made of charged particles, ionic compounds are electrically neutral overall, because the compound contains exactly enough of each ion for the charges to cancel.

Two names sort the common cases: if ionic bonds occur between metals and the nonmetal oxygen, **oxides** form; most other ionic compounds are called **salts**. **Binary ionic compounds** contain a metallic cation and a nonmetallic anion.

The **ionic bond** itself is the electrostatic force that holds the ions together in an ionic compound — an attraction between opposite charges, not a shared pair of electrons.

## Chemical formulae and formula units

A **chemical formula** shows the numbers of atoms of each element in the smallest representative unit of a substance. For an ionic compound that unit is the **formula unit**: the lowest whole-number ratio of ions in the compound.

For sodium chloride the lowest whole-number ratio of ions is 1:1 — one $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ ion to each $\mathrm{Cl^{-}}$ ion — so the formula unit is $\mathrm{NaCl}$. Although the ionic charges are used to derive the correct formula, they are not shown when you write the formula unit.

### Working out the ratio

Because the compound must be neutral, the charges of the cations and anions have to balance. The mechanical version of this is to reverse the numbers: for $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ one electron is taken and for $\mathrm{F^{-}}$ one electron is added, so reversing the numbers 1 and 1 gives the ratio 1:1.

Checking a finished formula is a matter of adding up the charges. For calcium fluoride, $\mathrm{CaF_{2}}$:

$$(+2) + 2 \times (-1) = 0$$

Reading a formula runs the same way in reverse. $\mathrm{Na_{2}O}$ is the formula for sodium oxide; within one formula unit of $\mathrm{Na_{2}O}$ there are 2 sodium ions and 1 oxide ion.

### Naming rule

Name of cation + name of anion. So the compound of $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^{-}}$ is sodium chloride.

## Coordination number

The **coordination number** of an ion is the number of ions of opposite charge that surround the ion in a crystal.

In $\mathrm{NaCl}$, each ion has a coordination number of 6: each $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ ion is surrounded by 6 $\mathrm{Cl^{-}}$ ions and each $\mathrm{Cl^{-}}$ ion is surrounded by 6 $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ ions. Note that this does not make the formula $\mathrm{Na_{6}Cl_{6}}$ — reduced to the lowest whole-number ratio, $\mathrm{Na_{6}Cl_{6}}$ is still $\mathrm{NaCl}$. The coordination number describes the geometry of the crystal; the formula unit describes the ratio.

## Properties of ionic compounds

Most ionic compounds are crystalline solids at room temperature, with the component ions arranged in repeating three-dimensional patterns. In that arrangement each ion is attracted strongly to each of its neighbours and repulsions are minimised — and the properties below all follow from it.

**Property 1: a very stable structure**, the result of the large attractive forces throughout the crystal.

**Property 2: high melting point.** The network of attractions extends throughout the whole ionic crystal, so ionic compounds have higher melting and boiling points than other types of compound, such as molecular compounds.

**Property 3: they break or shatter easily at room temperature.** When ionic crystals are struck, the cations and anions are shifted from their fixed positions, and the resulting repulsions between ions of like charge cause the crystal to shatter.

**Property 4: an ionic solid is a poor conductor**, but it conducts electricity in the molten (liquid) state and in the aqueous state, dissolved in water. In the solid the ions have fixed positions and no freedom to move. Melting breaks down the orderly crystal structure; dissolving frees the ions to move about in the solution. In both cases mobile charges appear, and mobile charges are what carrying a current requires.

$$\mathrm{NaCl(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl(molten)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na^{+}(molten)} + \mathrm{Cl^{-}(molten)}$$

$$\mathrm{NaCl(s)} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{H_2O}\ } \mathrm{NaCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na^{+}(aq)} + \mathrm{Cl^{-}(aq)}$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Ionic compound** | A compound composed of cations and anions, electrically neutral overall |
| **Oxide** | The compound formed when ionic bonds occur between a metal and the nonmetal oxygen |
| **Salt** | The name given to most ionic compounds other than oxides |
| **Binary ionic compound** | An ionic compound containing a metallic cation and a nonmetallic anion |
| **Ionic bond** | The electrostatic force that holds ions together in an ionic compound |
| **Chemical formula** | A formula showing the numbers of atoms of each element in the smallest representative unit of a substance |
| **Formula unit** | The lowest whole-number ratio of ions in an ionic compound |
| **Coordination number** | The number of ions of opposite charge that surround an ion in a crystal |

# 7.3 Bonding in Metals

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Metallic bonds

Metals consist of closely packed cations and loosely held valence electrons, rather than neutral atoms. The **electron sea model** proposes that all the metal atoms in a metallic solid contribute their valence electrons to form a "sea" of electrons. The electrons in metals that are free to move in this way are referred to as **delocalised electrons**.

**Metallic bonds** are the forces of attraction between the metallic cations and the delocalised electrons. The bonding is not directional and does not belong to any particular pair of atoms — which is exactly what the properties below depend on.

## Properties of metals

The typical physical properties of metals can be explained by the metallic bond, and they provide evidence of its strength.

**Melting and boiling points.** These vary greatly between metals: mercury is a liquid at room temperature, while tungsten has a melting point of 3422 degrees Celsius. In general, metals have moderately high melting points and high boiling points. The strength of metallic bonds depends on the charge and size of the cations, and it is that strength which sets properties such as melting and boiling point.

**Conduction.** Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity, because the mobile valence electrons always have the freedom to move.

**Ductility and malleability.** Metals are **ductile** (can be drawn into wires) and **malleable** (can be hammered or pressed into shapes). When a force is applied to a metal, the electrons shift and thereby keep the metal ions bonded in their new positions.

This is the cleanest contrast in the chapter. If an ionic crystal is struck with a hammer, the blow tends to push the positive ions close together; the positive ions repel one another and the crystal shatters. In a metal the sea of electrons simply flows with the ions, so the same blow reshapes the metal instead of destroying it. Same kind of impact, opposite outcome, because of the difference in bonding.

## Crystalline structure of metals

Metal atoms pack in three arrangements, distinguished by how many neighbours each atom has:

| Structure | Neighbours per atom | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Body-centred cubic | 8 (except those on the surface) | Na, K, Fe, Cr, W |
| Face-centred cubic | 12 | Cu, Ag, Au, Al, Pb |
| Hexagonal close-packed | 12 | Mg, Zn, Cd |

## Alloys

**Alloys** are mixtures of two or more elements, at least one of which is a metal. They are important because their properties are often superior to those of their component elements.

The most important alloys today are the **steels**, which have a wide range of useful properties: corrosion resistance, ductility, hardness and toughness.

Alloys come in two kinds, and which one forms depends on the relative sizes of the atoms involved:

| Type | Condition | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Substitutional alloy** | The atoms of the components are about the same size, so they can replace each other in the crystal | Sterling silver, brass, pewter |
| **Interstitial alloy** | The atomic sizes are quite different, so the smaller atoms fit into the interstices (spaces) between the larger atoms | Carbon steel |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Electron sea model** | The model proposing that all the metal atoms in a metallic solid contribute their valence electrons to form a "sea" of electrons |
| **Delocalised electrons** | The electrons in metals that are free to move |
| **Metallic bond** | The force of attraction between the metallic cations and the delocalised electrons |
| **Ductile** | Able to be drawn into wires |
| **Malleable** | Able to be hammered or pressed into shapes |
| **Alloy** | A mixture of two or more elements, at least one of which is a metal |
| **Substitutional alloy** | An alloy in which the component atoms are about the same size and replace each other in the crystal |
| **Interstitial alloy** | An alloy in which the atomic sizes differ, so the smaller atoms fit into the spaces between the larger atoms |

# 8.1 The Nature of Covalent Bonding

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Covalent bonds

A **covalent bond** is a bond formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons. It commonly occurs between nonmetals, or between metalloids. Where an ionic bond transfers electrons outright, a covalent bond leaves them jointly owned.

| Bond | Shared pairs | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Single bond** | One pair of electrons is shared | — |
| **Double bond** | Two shared pairs of electrons | $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ |

Double bonds appear where they are needed: in a structure like $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ the bonds effectively "move" to become multiple bonds because the atoms have to achieve an octet, and single bonds alone would not supply enough shared electrons.

## Drawing a Lewis structure

The procedure is short, and each step exists to satisfy a different constraint:

1. **Count the total number of valence electrons**, including any charges. This fixes how many electrons you have to place — a charged species has more or fewer than the neutral atoms alone would give.
2. **If there are remainder electrons, place them on the middle atom.**
3. **If the octets are not complete, form double or triple bonds.** Turning a lone pair into a shared pair lets one pair of electrons count towards two atoms' octets at once.

## Coordinate covalent bonds

A **coordinate covalent bond** is a type of covalent bond in which one atom provides both electrons for the shared pair.

It usually forms when one atom already has a lone pair of electrons available to donate. Polyatomic ions often contain a mixture of regular covalent bonds and coordinate covalent bonds.

## Exceptions to the octet rule

| Exception | What happens | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Odd number of electrons | The electrons cannot all be paired, so the octet rule cannot be satisfied | $\mathrm{NO_{2}}$ |
| Fewer than an octet | The central atom is left short of eight electrons | Boron in $\mathrm{BF_{3}}$, which has 3 surrounding atoms |
| More than an octet | The central atom has more than 4 surrounding atoms, so it ends up with more than eight electrons | $\mathrm{SF_{6}}$, in which the central sulfur has 12 electrons |

## Bond energy and bond length

Two related trends govern the strength of covalent bonds:

- Strong covalent bonds go with shorter bond lengths.
- Multiple bonds are shorter and stronger than single bonds, and a triple bond is shorter than a double bond.

The two statements are consistent with each other: a triple bond is the shortest of the three, and therefore also the strongest.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Covalent bond** | A bond formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons; commonly between nonmetals or metalloids |
| **Single bond** | A bond in which only one pair of electrons is shared |
| **Double bond** | A bond that involves two shared pairs of electrons |
| **Coordinate covalent bond** | A covalent bond in which one atom provides both electrons for the shared pair |

# 8.2 Molecular Compounds

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## I. Molecules and molecular compounds

A **molecule** is a neutral group of atoms joined together by covalent bonds. Neutral is the operative word — nothing has been transferred, so there is no charge to balance.

A **diatomic molecule** is a molecule that contains two atoms; an oxygen molecule is the standard example. Molecules can also be made of atoms of different elements, and a compound composed of molecules is called a **molecular compound**.

## II. Representing molecules

A **molecular formula** is the chemical formula of a molecular compound. It shows how many atoms of each element a substance contains, and it reflects the *actual* number of atoms in each molecule — so unlike the formula unit of an ionic compound, the subscripts are not necessarily the lowest whole-number ratios. Butane, $\mathrm{C_{4}H_{10}}$, is a molecular compound whose formula makes the point: $\mathrm{C_{4}H_{10}}$ would reduce to $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}}$ as a ratio, but the molecule really does contain four carbons and ten hydrogens.

What a molecular formula does not show is the molecule's structure. For that a model is needed. A **ball-and-stick model** shows the three-dimensional structure of a molecule: a ball represents an atom's nucleus and inner-level electrons, and sticks represent the bonds, with a straight stick for a single bond and curved springs for multiple bonds.

The arrangement of atoms within a molecule is called its **molecular structure**.

## III. Comparing molecular and ionic compounds

| | Molecular compound | Ionic compound |
|---|---|---|
| Representative unit | Molecule | Formula unit — the lowest whole-number ratio of ions |
| Melting and boiling points | Relatively lower; many are gases or liquids at room temperature | Relatively higher |
| Types of component element | Nonmetal + nonmetal | Metal + nonmetal |

The last row is the quickest classification test available: look at what kinds of element the formula contains, and the compound type follows.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Molecule** | A neutral group of atoms joined together by covalent bonds |
| **Diatomic molecule** | A molecule that contains two atoms |
| **Molecular compound** | A compound composed of molecules |
| **Molecular formula** | The chemical formula of a molecular compound; it shows the actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule |
| **Ball-and-stick model** | A model showing the three-dimensional structure of a molecule, with balls for nuclei and inner-level electrons and sticks for bonds |
| **Molecular structure** | The arrangement of atoms within a molecule |
| **Formula unit** | The lowest whole-number ratio of ions in an ionic compound |

# 8.3 Bonding Theories

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## I. VSEPR theory

A molecular formula says which atoms are present but nothing about how they sit in space. To explain the three-dimensional shape of molecules, scientists use **valence-shell electron-pair repulsion theory (VSEPR theory)**.

**VSEPR theory states that the repulsion between electron pairs causes molecular shapes to adjust so that the valence-electron pairs stay as far apart as possible.** In short: valence electron pairs move apart because they repel, and the shape you observe is whatever arrangement gets them furthest from one another.

The **bond angle** is the geometric angle between two adjacent bonds. It is the number that records the outcome of that spreading-out.

### The shapes

**Linear.** In a linear molecule the atoms can be connected by a straight line. Examples include $\mathrm{O_{2}}$, $\mathrm{N_{2}}$ and $\mathrm{HCl}$.

**Trigonal planar.** A trigonal planar molecule has a triangular, flat shape with 120 degree angles — for example boron trichloride, $\mathrm{BCl_{3}}$. The three pairs of electrons are arranged as far apart as possible.

**Tetrahedral.** A tetrahedral molecule has four surfaces and 109.5 degree angles, again because the four pairs of electrons are arranged as far apart as possible. The hydrogens in a methane molecule are at the four corners of a geometric solid called a regular tetrahedron, and in this arrangement all of the H–C–H angles are 109.5°. The same angle applies to other tetrahedral molecules.

**Pyramidal.** The four pairs of electrons are again arranged as far apart as possible, but the angle comes out at 107 degrees. The nitrogen in ammonia, $\mathrm{NH_{3}}$, is surrounded by four pairs of valence electrons, one of which is an unshared pair. That unshared pair strongly repels the bonding pairs, pushing them together.

This is the comparison the section is built around: both tetrahedral and pyramidal shapes have four pairs of electrons surrounding the central atom, and because the unshared pair exerts a greater repulsive force, the bond angle in the pyramidal shape is slightly less than in the tetrahedral shape. Put simply, unshared pairs "take up more space" and cause the others to "squeeze".

**Bent.** Four pairs of electrons arranged as far apart as possible, where the central atom is joined to two other atoms and has two unshared pairs. The bond angle in a bent shape is 105 degrees — smaller again, following the same logic, because there are now two unshared pairs doing the squeezing.

| Shape | Bond angle | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Linear | — | $\mathrm{O_{2}}$, $\mathrm{N_{2}}$, $\mathrm{HCl}$ |
| Trigonal planar | 120° | $\mathrm{BCl_{3}}$ |
| Tetrahedral | 109.5° | Methane |
| Pyramidal | 107° | $\mathrm{NH_{3}}$ |
| Bent | 105° | — |

Further shapes named in this section are trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral and square planar.

### The shape of larger molecules

The shape of a larger molecule is determined by the bond angle at each central atom — a big molecule is not one shape but a chain of local shapes. In the worked example the bond angle at the first carbon is 109.5° (tetrahedral), at the second carbon 120° (trigonal planar), and at the third atom, an oxygen, 105° (bent).

## II. Hybrid orbitals

When an atom approaches another atom to form a bond, the atomic orbitals mix together, forming **hybrid orbitals**. In **hybridisation**, several atomic orbitals mix to form the same total number of equivalent hybrid orbitals — the count is conserved, so mixing three orbitals produces three hybrids, never two or four.

| Molecular shape | Number of orbitals | Hybrid orbitals |
|---|---|---|
| Linear | 2 | $sp$ |
| Trigonal planar | 3 | $sp^{2}$ |
| Tetrahedral, pyramidal, bent (105°) | 4 | $sp^{3}$ |

The three shapes on the last row share a hybridisation because they share an electron-pair count: four pairs around the central atom in every case, differing only in how many of those pairs are unshared.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **VSEPR theory** | Valence-shell electron-pair repulsion theory: the repulsion between electron pairs causes molecular shapes to adjust so that the valence-electron pairs stay as far apart as possible |
| **Bond angle** | The geometric angle between two adjacent bonds |
| **Linear** | A shape in which the atoms can be connected by a straight line |
| **Trigonal planar** | A triangular, flat shape with 120° angles |
| **Tetrahedral** | A shape with four surfaces and 109.5° angles |
| **Pyramidal** | A four-electron-pair shape with one unshared pair and a bond angle of 107° |
| **Bent** | A four-electron-pair shape with two other atoms and two unshared pairs, and a bond angle of 105° |
| **Hybrid orbitals** | Orbitals formed when atomic orbitals mix together as an atom approaches another atom to form a bond |
| **Hybridisation** | The mixing of several atomic orbitals to form the same total number of equivalent hybrid orbitals |

# 8.4 Polar Bonds and Molecules

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## I. Bond polarity

The bonding pairs of electrons in covalent bonds are pulled between the nuclei of the atoms sharing them — both nuclei pull on the shared electrons. Whether the tug-of-war is even decides the character of the bond.

- A **nonpolar bond** is a covalent bond formed when the atoms in the bond pull equally, so the bond electrons are shared equally.
- A **polar bond** is a covalent bond between atoms in which the electrons are shared unequally.

The difference in electronegativity between the two atoms is what decides this, and it does so on a sliding scale that runs all the way into ionic bonding:

| Electronegativity difference | Bond type |
|---|---|
| $\le 0.4$ | Nonpolar covalent |
| $0.4 < \Delta\mathrm{EN} < 2.0$ | Polar covalent |
| $\ge 2.0$ | Ionic |

The table is worth reading as a continuum rather than three separate categories: an ionic bond is the limiting case of an extremely unequal share.

## II. Describing polar covalent bonds

The lowercase Greek letter delta ($\delta$) denotes that the atoms in a covalent bond acquire only **partial charges** — less than $1+$ or $1-$. These partial charges are shown as clouds of electron density.

In hydrogen chloride, the chlorine atom attracts the electron cloud more than the hydrogen atom does, so the bond is written

$$\overset{\delta+}{\mathrm{H}} \text{—} \overset{\delta-}{\mathrm{Cl}}$$

The polar nature of a bond may also be represented by an arrow pointing towards the more electronegative atom.

## III. Determining the polarity of molecules

A molecule containing only nonpolar bonds is a **nonpolar molecule**. But a molecule containing polar bonds is *not* necessarily a polar molecule — this is the point most often got wrong. **The shape of a molecule and the polarity of its bonds together determine whether the molecule is polar or nonpolar**, because equal pulls in opposite directions cancel out.

| Type | Molecular shape | Are all outside atoms the same? | Molecular polarity |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{AX_{2}}$ | Linear | Yes | Nonpolar |
| $\mathrm{AX_{2}}$ | Linear | No | Polar |
| $\mathrm{AX_{2}}$ | Bent | — | Polar |
| $\mathrm{AX_{3}}$ | Trigonal planar | Yes | Nonpolar |
| $\mathrm{AX_{3}}$ | Trigonal planar | No | Polar |
| $\mathrm{AX_{3}}$ | Pyramidal | — | Polar |
| $\mathrm{AX_{4}}$ | Tetrahedral | Yes | Nonpolar |
| $\mathrm{AX_{4}}$ | Tetrahedral | No | Polar |

Notice that the bent and pyramidal shapes are polar regardless of the outside atoms: their shapes are not symmetrical, so nothing cancels.

## IV. Attractions between molecules

**Van der Waals forces** are the two weakest attractions between molecules, also known as intermolecular forces.

**Dipole interactions** occur when polar molecules are attracted to one another: the slightly negative region of a polar molecule is weakly attracted to the slightly positive region of another polar molecule. They are similar to ionic bonds, but much weaker — the charges involved are partial, not full.

**Dispersion forces** are caused by the motion of electrons. They are the weakest of all molecular interactions, but they operate between all molecules, occurring even between nonpolar ones. Their strength generally increases as the number of electrons in a molecule increases, which follows from their cause: more electrons in motion means more of the fluctuation that produces the force.

**Hydrogen bonding** is an especially strong dipole–dipole force between the hydrogen atom of one molecule ($\delta+$) and the N, O or F atom of another molecule ($\delta-$). The guide lists the partners as "F, O, S, or N"; that is an error — only N, O and F are electronegative enough to form hydrogen bonds, and sulfur does not belong on the list. The positive region of one water molecule attracts the negative region of another water molecule. Hydrogen bonds are the strongest of the intermolecular forces, and they are extremely important in determining the properties of water and of biological molecules — a snowflake's shape, for instance, is determined by the interactions of hydrogen bonds during its formation.

| Force | Relative strength | Where it operates |
|---|---|---|
| Dispersion forces | Weakest of all molecular interactions | Between all molecules, including nonpolar ones |
| Dipole interactions | Weak; much weaker than ionic bonds | Between polar molecules |
| Hydrogen bonding | Strongest of the intermolecular forces | Between an H atom ($\delta+$) and an N, O or F atom ($\delta-$) on another molecule |

## V. Intermolecular attractions and molecular properties

The diversity of physical properties among covalent compounds is mainly because of their widely varying intermolecular attractions. The melting and boiling points of most molecular compounds are low compared with those of ionic compounds, because in most solids formed by molecules only the weak attractions *between* molecules need to be broken — the covalent bonds within each molecule survive melting untouched.

A few solids consisting of molecules do not melt until the temperature reaches 1000 °C or higher. Most of these very stable substances are **network solids** (or network crystals), solids in which all of the atoms are covalently bonded to each other. Here there are no weak intermolecular attractions to break; melting would mean breaking covalent bonds throughout the whole crystal.

**Diamond.** Each carbon atom in a diamond is covalently bonded to four other carbons, interconnecting the carbon atoms throughout the diamond. Diamond does not melt at all; rather, it vaporises to a gas at 3500 °C and above.

**Silicon dioxide (quartz)** has a giant covalent structure similar to diamond. Each silicon atom (2.8.4) is bonded to four oxygen atoms, and each oxygen atom (2.6) is bonded to two silicon atoms.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Nonpolar bond** | A covalent bond formed when the atoms in the bond pull equally and the bond electrons are shared equally |
| **Polar bond** | A covalent bond between atoms in which the electrons are shared unequally |
| **Partial charge ($\delta$)** | A charge less than $1+$ or $1-$ acquired by an atom in a polar covalent bond |
| **Nonpolar molecule** | A molecule containing only nonpolar bonds |
| **Van der Waals forces** | The two weakest attractions between molecules; also known as intermolecular forces |
| **Dipole interactions** | Attractions occurring when the slightly negative region of a polar molecule is attracted to the slightly positive region of another |
| **Dispersion forces** | Forces caused by the motion of electrons; the weakest of all molecular interactions, operating between all molecules |
| **Hydrogen bonding** | An especially strong dipole–dipole force between the hydrogen atom of one molecule ($\delta+$) and the N, O or F atom of another ($\delta-$); the strongest intermolecular force |
| **Network solid (network crystal)** | A solid in which all of the atoms are covalently bonded to each other |

# 9.1-9.3 Naming Ionic Compounds and Molecular Compounds

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## 1. Monatomic ions

**Monatomic ions** consist of a single atom with a positive or negative charge resulting from the loss or gain of one or more valence electrons.

- The names of **cations** are the same as the elements, followed by the word *ion* or *cation*.
- The names of **anions** start with the stem of the element name and end in *–ide*.

Some metals form more than one ion, so the name has to say which. Two methods are used:

| Method | How it works | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Stock system** | Place a Roman numeral in parentheses | $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} \rightarrow$ iron(II) ion; $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}} \rightarrow$ iron(III) ion |
| **Root word** | Use the older Latin-based stem with a suffix | $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} \rightarrow$ ferrous ion; $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}} \rightarrow$ ferric ion |

## 2. Polyatomic ions

**Polyatomic ions** are composed of more than one atom. They behave as a unit and carry a charge.

Where a family of polyatomic ions differs only in the number of oxygen atoms, the prefix and suffix encode that number. Chlorine's oxyanions show the whole ladder at once:

| Number of oxygen atoms | Name pattern | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Greatest | prefix *per–* plus suffix *–ate* | Perchlorate, $\mathrm{ClO_{4}^{-}}$ |
| More | suffix *–ate* | Chlorate, $\mathrm{ClO_{3}^{-}}$ |
| Fewer | suffix *–ite* | Chlorite, $\mathrm{ClO_{2}^{-}}$ |
| Fewest | prefix *hypo–* plus suffix *–ite* | Hypochlorite, $\mathrm{ClO^{-}}$ |

Note that *hypo–* is pronounced the same as "hypa".

## 3. Binary ionic compounds

To **write** the formula of a binary ionic compound, first write the symbol of the cation and then that of the anion, then add subscripts as needed to balance the charge. The mechanical shortcut for this is the **crisscross method**: each ion's charge becomes the other ion's subscript, giving $\mathrm{A_{x}B_{y}}$.

To **name** any binary ionic compound, place the cation name first, followed by the anion name. If the metallic element in the compound has more than one common ionic charge, a Roman numeral must be included — for example $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ is copper(II).

## 4. Compounds with polyatomic ions

Whenever more than one polyatomic ion is needed to balance the charges in an ionic compound, use parentheses to set off the polyatomic ion in the formula. Without them the subscript would appear to apply to only one element of the ion rather than to the whole group.

## 5. Binary molecular compounds

Molecular compounds are named differently, because two nonmetals can combine in several different ratios and the name has to distinguish them. The rules are:

1. Write the names of the elements in the order listed in the formula.
2. Use prefixes appropriately to indicate the number of each kind of atom.
3. End the name of the second element with the suffix *–ide*. For example, carbon tetrabromide is $\mathrm{CBr_{4}}$.

Two refinements to the prefixes:

- If just one atom of the first element is in the formula, omit the prefix *mono–* for that element. Carbon monoxide is $\mathrm{CO}$ — *mono–* appears on the oxygen but not on the carbon.
- The vowel at the end of a prefix is sometimes dropped when the name of the element begins with a vowel: *pentoxide*, not *pentaoxide*.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Monatomic ion** | An ion consisting of a single atom with a positive or negative charge resulting from the loss or gain of one or more valence electrons |
| **Stock system** | A naming system that places a Roman numeral in parentheses to show the charge of a metal that forms more than one ion |
| **Polyatomic ion** | An ion composed of more than one atom, which behaves as a unit and carries a charge |
| **Crisscross method** | The method of writing a binary ionic formula $\mathrm{A_{x}B_{y}}$ by using each ion's charge as the other's subscript |

An **acid** is a compound that contains one or more hydrogen atoms and produces hydrogen ions when dissolved in water. Both halves of that definition matter: the hydrogen has to be there in the formula, and it has to be released as ions in water.

A **base** is a compound that produces hydroxide ions when dissolved in water. A base is generally an ionic compound, which is why bases are named by the ordinary ionic rules rather than by any special scheme.

The name of the cation is followed by the name of the anion.

# 6.1 Wave Nature of Light

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Everything in this chapter is an attempt to answer one question: where exactly are the electrons in an atom, and what are they doing? The answer turns out to depend on the behaviour of light, so the chapter starts there.

## Light as an electromagnetic wave

Light is a kind of **electromagnetic radiation**. An electromagnetic wave consists of an electric field and a magnetic field oscillating at right angles to each other.

The SI unit for **frequency** is the hertz, $\mathrm{Hz}$.

The **electromagnetic spectrum** separates waves into different levels. Within the part of it we can see, the **wavelength** of the waves of the visible spectrum increases in the following order:

$$\text{violet} < \text{indigo} < \text{blue} < \text{green} < \text{yellow} < \text{orange} < \text{red}$$

Frequency and energy run the other way: violet has the highest frequency and the greatest energy, and red the lowest frequency and the least energy. The guide prints this one order for wavelength, frequency and energy alike; that is an error — the order above holds for wavelength only, and frequency and energy increase from red back to violet.

## Where the wave model breaks down

The wave model is not a complete description. It does not explain how light can form when temperature increases — the effect you see in neon lights. This failure is what forces the introduction of the quantum idea.

A **quantum** is the smallest amount of energy. The energy of one quantum is

$$E = h\nu$$

where $\nu$ is the frequency of the radiation and $h$ is Planck's constant. Because energy comes in whole quanta rather than in a smooth stream, the amount of energy carried by radiation of a given frequency is fixed.

## The photoelectric effect

In the **photoelectric effect**, electrons are ejected when light shines on a metal. The photon delivers its energy to the electron, part of that energy is spent getting the electron out of the metal, and whatever is left over becomes the electron's motion:

$$KE = E_{\text{photon}} - E_{\text{threshold}}$$

The threshold term is the reason the effect has a cut-off: if the photon's energy is below it, there is nothing left over and no electron leaves.

## The hydrogen line spectrum

Electrons can be **excited** to higher energy levels when they absorb energy. When the atom is in an **excited state**, the electron can drop from a higher energy level back to a lower one. As a result, the atom emits a photon corresponding to the difference between the energies associated with the two orbits.

This is why the hydrogen spectrum is a set of sharp lines rather than a continuous band: **only certain frequencies of radiation can be emitted**, because only certain energy differences exist between the levels. Combined with $E = h\nu$, a fixed set of energy gaps gives a fixed set of frequencies.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Electromagnetic radiation** | The class of radiation to which light belongs; an electromagnetic wave consists of electric and magnetic fields oscillating at right angles |
| **Hertz ($\mathrm{Hz}$)** | The SI unit for frequency |
| **Electromagnetic spectrum** | The arrangement that separates waves into different levels |
| **Quantum** | The smallest amount of energy |
| **Photoelectric effect** | Electrons are ejected when light shines on a metal |
| **Excited state** | The state of an atom whose electron has absorbed energy and been raised to a higher energy level |

# 6.4 The Wave Nature of Matter and Quantum Mechanics

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Light behaves as a wave in some experiments and as a stream of particles in others. This section takes that duality and turns it round: if a wave can behave like a particle, can a particle behave like a wave?

## De Broglie's theory

Louis de Broglie theorised that **if light can have material properties, matter should exhibit wave properties**. The suggestion is symmetric — it does not single light out as a special case, and it means an electron in an atom must be treated as something with a wavelength rather than as a small ball on a track.

## The Heisenberg uncertainty principle

The **Heisenberg uncertainty principle** states that the position and the velocity of a moving electron at one point cannot be measured at the same time.

This is not a limitation of laboratory equipment that better instruments would remove. It is why the fixed orbits of the Bohr model cannot survive: an orbit is precisely a claim about where an electron is *and* how fast it is going.

## Quantum mechanics

This section is flagged in the guide as **VERY IMPORTANT**.

Schrödinger found the **quantum mechanical model**. The model has three properties, and each one is inherited from a piece of physics established earlier:

| Property of the model | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| The energy of an electron is quantised | The Bohr model |
| Electrons exhibit wavelike behaviour | De Broglie |
| The exact position as well as the momentum/velocity of an electron at any given point is impossible to know | The Heisenberg uncertainty principle |

Solutions to the Schrödinger equation lead to a mathematical expression called an **atomic orbital**.

## Bohr model against the quantum mechanical model

There are differences between the two models:

| Bohr model | Quantum mechanical model |
|---|---|
| Electrons exist in fixed orbits and pathways | Electrons exist in a probability-based region of the atom |

The shift from "pathway" to "probability-based region" is the whole point of the change. Once the uncertainty principle rules out knowing position and velocity together, the best any model can offer is a region in which the electron is likely to be found.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **De Broglie's theory** | If light can have material properties, matter should exhibit wave properties |
| **Heisenberg uncertainty principle** | The position and the velocity of a moving electron at one point cannot be measured at the same time |
| **Quantum mechanical model** | Schrödinger's model of the atom, in which the electron's energy is quantised, the electron behaves as a wave, and its exact position and momentum cannot both be known |
| **Atomic orbital** | The mathematical expression obtained from solutions to the Schrödinger equation |

# 6.6 Representation of Orbitals

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The quantum mechanical model provides the theory for the existence of different atomic orbitals. This section is about what those orbitals are and how many of each kind exist.

## The four types of orbital

Atomic orbitals are classified as **s**, **p**, **d** and **f**.

Each orbital can hold **no more than 2 electrons**.

For every principal energy level, there are 1, 3, 5 and 7 orbitals for the s, p, d and f shells respectively, because the orientation of the shells may be different in a three-dimensional plane. The count is a count of orientations: there is only one way to place an s orbital, but seven distinguishable ways to place an f orbital in space.

| Shell | Number of orbitals | Maximum electrons |
|---|---|---|
| s | 1 | 2 |
| p | 3 | 6 |
| d | 5 | 10 |
| f | 7 | 14 |

The maximum-electron column follows directly from the two-per-orbital limit.

## The principal quantum number

The **principal quantum number**, $n$, always equals the number of sublevels within that principal energy level. So $n = 1$ has one sublevel available to it, $n = 2$ has two, and so on — which is why the s sublevel appears first and the f sublevel does not appear until $n$ has grown large enough to accommodate it.

## Critical thinking

The guide leaves a question for you to work on: how does the size and shape of the orbitals change as the principal quantum number changes in a hydrogen molecule? What about in a multi-electron system?

The distinction between the two cases matters, and it returns in the next section — the structure of a hydrogen atom and the structure of a multi-electron atom are not the same problem.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Atomic orbital** | A region described by the quantum mechanical model, classified as s, p, d or f, holding no more than 2 electrons |
| **Principal quantum number ($n$)** | The number that always equals the number of sublevels within that principal energy level |

# 6.7 Electron Structure of Atoms

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Notice before starting that there is a difference in structure between a hydrogen atom and a multi-electron atom. Once more than one electron is present, the electrons interact with each other and the orbitals of a given principal energy level no longer all sit at the same energy.

## Degenerate orbitals and the filling pattern

**Degenerate orbitals** are orbitals with the same energy.

The electron structure of atoms follows a pattern, going from s to p to d and then to f, as the energy of each orbital increases with the principal quantum number.

## The three rules

The guide is emphatic here: **these rules are important and definitely will be on the test.**

**The Aufbau principle.** Electrons occupy orbitals of the lower energy first. Within the same principal quantum level the orbitals are ordered

$$s < p < d < f$$

so an electron entering a shell takes the s sublevel before the p, the p before the d, and so on.

**The Pauli exclusion principle.** No two electrons in the same atom can have the same quantum number. The quantum number is divided into many portions — think of them as the different conditions used to identify an electron: its principal quantum number, its type of orbital, its direction of spin, and so on. Because those conditions must not all coincide, **no two electrons in the same orbital can have the same direction of spin**, and therefore each orbital can hold only 2 electrons. The two-electron limit from the previous section is not an extra rule; it is a consequence of this one.

**Hund's rule.** For degenerate orbitals, the lowest energy is attained when the number of electrons with the same spin is maximised. In practice: for each orbital of the same energy, the number of electrons with the same spin must be greatest. This is what makes you spread electrons singly across a set of p orbitals before pairing any of them up.

## Writing electron configurations

**Electron configuration** is the arrangement of electrons into the different subshells of different energy levels in the quantum mechanical model. The electrons are arranged from lower to higher energy levels, as the Aufbau principle requires.

Reading a term such as $3p^5$:

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| The first number | The principal quantum number |
| The letter | The orbital type |
| The superscript on the right | The number of electrons in that subshell |

The configuration of electrons is difficult to explain and requires a lot of practice to understand. You should know how to do your homework.

## Abbreviated configurations

The configuration of an element can be written as the closest noble gas element — which must be smaller than the element itself — followed by the additional subshells. For example:

$$\mathrm{Cl}: [\mathrm{Ne}]\,3s^2\,3p^5$$

The inner-shell electrons are the **core electrons**. The electrons written after the noble-gas core are the **outer-shell electrons**. The outer-shell electrons include the electrons involved in chemical bonding, which are the **valence electrons**. This is why the abbreviated form is the more useful one for bonding work: it strips out exactly the electrons that do not take part.

## Two configurations to know

$$\mathrm{Cr}: 1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\,3d^5\,4s^1$$

$$\mathrm{Cu}: 1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\,3d^{10}\,4s^1$$

In both cases the 4s subshell holds a single electron rather than the pair a straight application of the filling order would give.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Degenerate orbitals** | Orbitals with the same energy |
| **Aufbau principle** | Electrons occupy orbitals of the lower energy first |
| **Pauli exclusion principle** | No two electrons in the same atom can have the same quantum number |
| **Hund's rule** | For degenerate orbitals, the lowest energy is attained when the number of electrons with the same spin is maximised |
| **Electron configuration** | The arrangement of electrons into the different subshells of different energy levels in a quantum mechanical model |
| **Abbreviated configuration** | A configuration written as the closest noble gas smaller than the element, plus the additional subshells following it |
| **Core electrons** | The inner-shell electrons |
| **Outer-shell electrons** | The electrons given after the noble-gas core |
| **Valence electrons** | The outer-shell electrons involved in chemical bonding |

# 6.8 Uncertainty, Significant Figures and Dimensional Analysis

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Two laboratory skills sit alongside the theory of this chapter: knowing how far to trust a measurement, and knowing how to check that an equation makes sense at all.

## Uncertainty

Measurements in chemistry might be inaccurate by eye. This creates **uncertainty** — being unsure of the exact value of something.

The uncertainty is calculated as **half of the scale graduations**. A burette marked every $0.1\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ therefore carries an uncertainty of $0.05\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, because that is the finest distinction the scale allows you to make by eye.

## Error

To evaluate the accuracy of experimental data, calculate the difference between the experimental value and the accepted value:

$$\text{Error} = \text{experimental value} - \text{accepted value}$$

Error can be negative. The sign is information — it tells you which side of the accepted value you fell on — so do not discard it.

## Systematic and random error

**Systematic error** comes from procedures, methods or theories. Its sources include:

- an incorrectly zeroed balance
- poorly calibrated or badly made instruments
- instrument parallax error — reading a scale from a position that is not directly in front of the scale
- improper conditions

**Systematic errors cannot be reduced by repetition.** If the balance reads high every time, averaging a hundred readings only gives you a very precise wrong answer.

The error associated with estimating the last digit of a reading is called **random uncertainty**. Random uncertainties arise mostly from limitations in the instrument.

## Percentage uncertainty

The **percentage uncertainty** changes with the amount of material that you are measuring. The absolute uncertainty of a piece of apparatus is fixed by its scale, so measuring a larger quantity with the same apparatus makes that fixed uncertainty a smaller fraction of the result.

Percentage uncertainty is also a guiding factor in choosing equipment for an experiment — it is the quantity you compare when deciding which instrument is good enough for the measurement you need.

## Dimensional analysis

**Dimensions** are the fundamental types of physical quantities.

The main idea of **dimensional analysis** is to check the consistency of equations and to help in deriving relationships between physical quantities. It is like a grammar check for the language of physics and engineering equations: an equation whose two sides do not carry the same dimensions cannot be right, whatever the numbers say.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Uncertainty** | Being unsure of the exact value of something; calculated as half of the scale graduations |
| **Error** | The experimental value minus the accepted value; can be negative |
| **Systematic error** | Error coming from procedures, methods or theories; it cannot be reduced by repetition |
| **Parallax error** | Reading a scale from a position that is not directly in front of the scale |
| **Random uncertainty** | The error associated with estimating the last digit of a reading; arises mostly from limitations in the instrument |
| **Percentage uncertainty** | An uncertainty expressed as a percentage; it changes with the amount of material being measured and guides the choice of equipment |
| **Dimensions** | The fundamental types of physical quantities |
| **Dimensional analysis** | Checking the consistency of equations and deriving relationships between physical quantities |
