# 7.1 Development of the Periodic Table

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The periodic table was not designed; it was noticed. The story below is a sequence in which each step supplies something the previous step was missing.

## The elements are counted

In the **1790s**, Antoine Lavoisier compiled a list of 23 elements known at the time. By **1870** there were approximately 70 known elements.

That growth is what made organisation urgent. Twenty-three substances can simply be listed; seventy cannot be held in the head without some structure.

## Atomic mass becomes measurable

In the **1860s**, chemists developed and agreed upon a method of determining the atomic mass of elements.

This is the enabling step for everything that follows. Without an agreed method there is no shared quantity to order the elements by, and so no way to see a pattern.

## Newlands sees a repetition

In **1864**, John Newlands observed the repetition of properties in every eight elements. This demonstrates a **periodic** change, because it repeats in a specific manner.

## Mendeleev and Meyer

In **1869**, Dmitri Mendeleev and Lothar Meyer both demonstrated a connection between atomic mass and elemental properties.

Mendeleev was given more credit because he was the earliest to publish his organisation plan and demonstrated how it was useful. Priority of publication and demonstrated usefulness, rather than the discovery itself, are what separate the two names.

Mendeleev noticed that **when the elements were ordered by increasing atomic mass, there was a repetition, or periodic pattern, in their chemical and physical properties.**

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Periodic change** | A change that repeats in a specific manner, as with the repetition of properties Newlands observed in every eight elements |

# 7.2 Effective Nuclear Charge and the Sizes of Atoms and Ions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

One quantity drives the periodic trends in this chapter. Establish it first and the size trends fall out of it.

## Effective nuclear charge

**Effective nuclear charge** is the net positive charge experienced by the valence electrons, accounting for the nuclear charge and the shielding by inner electrons.

Its trends:

| Direction | Effective nuclear charge |
|---|---|
| Across a period | Increases |
| Down a group | Increases slightly |

The contrast between "increases" and "increases slightly" is the important part. Across a period the nucleus gains protons while the shielding inner shell stays the same, so the valence electrons feel much more pull. Down a group protons are added too, but so is a whole new shielding layer, so the net gain is small.

## Atomic radius

| Direction | Atomic radius |
|---|---|
| Across a period | Decreases |
| Down a group | Increases |

The across-a-period result is the counterintuitive one, and it is exactly what the effective nuclear charge predicts: adding electrons to the same shell while the effective nuclear charge rises pulls that shell in tighter, so the atom gets smaller.

## Ionic radius

**Cations are smaller than their parent atoms**, because the loss of electrons reduces repulsion. Fewer electrons in the cloud means less pushing apart, and the remainder are drawn in closer.

## Isoelectronic series

In an **isoelectronic series** — species with the same number of electrons — size decreases with increasing nuclear charge. With the electron count held fixed, the only variable left is how hard the nucleus pulls, so the species with the most protons is the smallest.

## Worked example

Which is the largest atom among $\mathrm{Na}$, $\mathrm{Be}$ and $\mathrm{Mg}$?

$\mathrm{Na}$ — it is in Group 1 and Period 3. It sits furthest down and furthest left of the three, which is the corner in which both trends point towards the largest radius.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Effective nuclear charge** | The net positive charge experienced by valence electrons, accounting for nuclear charge and shielding by inner electrons |
| **Atomic radius** | The size of an atom; decreases across a period and increases down a group |
| **Ionic radius** | The size of an ion; cations are smaller than their parent atoms because losing electrons reduces repulsion |
| **Isoelectronic series** | A set of species in which size decreases with increasing nuclear charge |

# 7.4 Ionisation Energy, Electron Affinity and Electronegativity

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Three quantities describe how an atom handles electrons: what it costs to take one away, what happens when one is added, and how hard it pulls on the electrons in a bond it has already formed.

## Ionisation energy

**Ionisation energy** is the energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom. The "gaseous" condition matters — it fixes the atom as isolated, so the value measures the atom itself and not its neighbours.

| Direction | Ionisation energy |
|---|---|
| Across a period | Increases |
| Down a group | Decreases |

Both follow the effective nuclear charge: a more strongly held electron is a more expensive electron to remove.

### The exception

There is a break in the across-a-period increase **between Groups IIA and IIIA** — for example $\mathrm{Be} > \mathrm{B}$, where the later element has the *lower* ionisation energy.

The reason is which electron is being removed. In Group IIIA the electron taken out is a p electron, which sits at higher energy, whereas in Group IIA it is an s electron. A higher-energy electron is less tightly bound, so removing it costs less even though the nuclear charge has gone up.

## Electron affinity

**Electron affinity** is the energy change when an electron is added to a gaseous atom. It is the mirror image of ionisation energy: one measures adding an electron to an isolated atom, the other removing one.

## Electronegativity

**Electronegativity** is the ability of an atom to attract electrons in a bond.

| Direction | Electronegativity |
|---|---|
| Across a period | Increases |
| Down a group | Decreases |

The across-a-period increase is again the effective nuclear charge at work — a higher effective nuclear charge means a stronger pull on any electron nearby, including one being shared in a bond.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Ionisation energy** | The energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom |
| **Electron affinity** | The energy change when an electron is added to a gaseous atom |
| **Electronegativity** | The ability of an atom to attract electrons in a bond |

# 8.1 Lewis Symbols and the Octet Rule

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What a chemical bond is

A **chemical bond** is the electrostatic attraction force that holds two atoms together. All three bond types below are versions of that one idea; they differ only in which charged things are being attracted to which.

| Bond type | Attraction between |
|---|---|
| **Ionic bond** | Cations and anions |
| **Covalent bond** | The nucleus and shared electrons |
| **Metallic bond** | Metal cations and delocalised electrons |

## The octet rule

The **octet rule** is the tendency for electrons to achieve a noble gas configuration — "octet" refers to 8 valence electrons.

This is the rule that predicts what an atom will do in a bond: whether it gives electrons away, takes them, or shares them depends on which route gets it to a noble gas configuration fastest.

## Lewis symbols

**Lewis symbols** are a drawing method that serves as an alternative to electron configuration. They are used to express chemical bonding and molecular geometry and to demonstrate valence.

To draw one:

1. Write the element — for example $\mathrm{H}$.
2. Determine the number of valence electrons — $\mathrm{H}$ has 1.
3. Draw one dot for each valence electron. For $\mathrm{H}$, with only one valence electron, only one dot is needed.
4. For most cases, the valence electrons should be as spread out on the four sides of the letter as possible. This is Hund's rule applied to the drawing: electrons occupy separate positions before they pair up.

Exceptions to the spreading rule are not considered in the test.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Chemical bond** | The electrostatic attraction force that holds two atoms together |
| **Ionic bond** | Attraction between cations and anions |
| **Covalent bond** | Attraction between the nucleus and shared electrons |
| **Metallic bond** | Attraction between metal cations and delocalised electrons |
| **Octet rule** | The tendency for electrons to achieve a noble gas configuration, "octet" referring to 8 valence electrons |
| **Lewis symbols** | A drawing method alternative to electron configuration, used to express chemical bonding and molecular geometry and to demonstrate valence |

# 8.2 Ionic Bonding

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Why ions form

Because of the octet rule, atoms want to gain or lose electrons to reach a noble gas configuration.

| Action | Result | Charge |
|---|---|---|
| Losing electrons | Cation | Positive |
| Gaining electrons | Anion | Negative |

Which way an atom goes is decided by whichever is the shorter route. Halogens (Group 17) have 7 valence electrons and need only 1 more to complete the octet, so they most often appear as anions with a $1-$ charge.

> **Tip for the test:** check the periodic table before you do bonding questions. The group number tells you the valence count, and the valence count tells you the charge.

## The pseudo-noble gas exception

For elements from Group 1B through 4A in Periods 4 to 6, the ions form by adopting a **pseudo-noble gas notation**, which is relatively stable as well. Examples include $\mathrm{Zn}$, $\mathrm{Pb}$ and $\mathrm{Ag}$.

These elements do not reach a true noble gas configuration, but the arrangement they do reach is stable enough to be the one that forms.

## Ionic compounds

An **ionic compound** can be described simply as the bond between cations and anions. The cations give electrons to the anions, creating an electrostatic force that bonds the two together.

Ionic compounds **must be neutral** — the charges of the cations and anions must balance. This is the constraint that fixes the formula: it is why the compound of a $2+$ cation and a $1-$ anion has two anions per cation and not one.

> **Tip for the test:** when asked to explain trends of ionic bonds, refer to Coulomb's Law.

## Lattice structures

Ionic compounds exist in groups. When they are grouped together the pattern is always $+-+-+-\ldots$, which makes it look like a lattice — a **lattice structure**.

## Properties

- Ionic compounds have a **high melting point** and **hardness**.
- Ionic compounds are **brittle**.

Both properties trace back to the same alternating lattice. The regular $+-+-$ arrangement means every ion is surrounded by oppositely charged neighbours, which is a great deal of electrostatic attraction to overcome — hence the high melting point and hardness. But the arrangement is also rigid, which is why a force that disturbs it shatters the solid rather than bending it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Cation** | An ion formed by losing electrons, carrying a positive charge |
| **Anion** | An ion formed by gaining electrons, carrying a negative charge |
| **Pseudo-noble gas notation** | The relatively stable configuration adopted by ions of elements from Group 1B through 4A in Periods 4 to 6, such as $\mathrm{Zn}$, $\mathrm{Pb}$ and $\mathrm{Ag}$ |
| **Ionic compound** | The bond between cations and anions, in which cations give electrons to anions and an electrostatic force bonds the two together |
| **Lattice structure** | The $+-+-+-$ pattern formed when ionic compounds are grouped together |

# 8.3 Covalent Bonds

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Before starting, review the definition of valence electrons — the whole of covalent bonding is an account of what those electrons do when neither atom is willing to hand them over.

## When covalent bonding happens

Covalent bonding occurs when atoms have quite high electronegativities. Neither atom will surrender an electron outright, so the electrons are shared instead.

> **Critical thinking:** given that, what properties do the elements involved in covalent bonds have?

The guide also sets out the general trend in how many covalent bonds different elements form, and asks: what conclusion can you draw from that trend?

## Sigma and pi bonds

Covalent bonds are classified by shape into **sigma ($\sigma$)** and **pi ($\pi$)** bonds.

**Sigma bonds** have the overlap of electrons focused on the intermolecular axis. The electron density is concentrated in the middle, directly between the two nuclei.

**Pi bonds** only occur in p orbitals. The p shells overlap vertically, forming two sausage-shaped clouds of electrons parallel to the intermolecular axis.

**Pi bonds have less energy because they have more repulsion.** The electron density in a $\pi$ bond sits off to the sides rather than between the nuclei, so the arrangement is less favourable than the head-on overlap of a $\sigma$ bond.

## Multiple bonds

Covalent bonds can exist as double or triple bonds. Every bond between two atoms contains exactly one $\sigma$ bond; the extra bonds of a multiple bond are all $\pi$.

| Bond | Composition |
|---|---|
| Single | 1 $\sigma$ |
| Double | 1 $\sigma$ + 1 $\pi$ |
| Triple | 1 $\sigma$ + 2 $\pi$ |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Sigma ($\sigma$) bond** | A bond whose electron overlap is focused on the intermolecular axis, with the electron density in the middle |
| **Pi ($\pi$) bond** | A bond occurring only in p orbitals, where the p shells overlap vertically to form two sausage-shaped clouds of electrons parallel to the intermolecular axis; it has less energy than a sigma bond because it has more repulsion |

# 8.4 Bond Polarity and Electronegativity

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Bond polarity

**Bond polarity** is a measure of how equally or unequally the electrons in any covalent bond are shared. In a **polar covalent bond**, one of the atoms exerts a greater attraction for the bonding electrons than the other.

**Polarity** refers to a separation of positive and negative charge.

- In a **nonpolar bond**, the bonding electrons are shared equally — diatomic molecules are the clearest case, since the two atoms are identical and neither can out-pull the other.
- In a **polar bond**, electrons are shared unequally.

## Electronegativity

In general, electronegativity values **decrease from top to bottom** and **increase from left to right**.

> **Test tip:** do not explain questions through direct trends. Focus instead on the reasons behind the trends — that requires critical thinking, and it is what the question is actually testing.

## Using the electronegativity difference

The electronegativity difference on the Pauling scale determines the type of bond:

| $\Delta EN$ | Bond type |
|---|---|
| $> 2.0$ | Ionic |
| $0.4 - 2.0$ | Polar covalent |
| $< 0.4$ | Nonpolar covalent |

The boundaries make sense as a continuum rather than three separate phenomena: a large enough difference in pulling power means one atom has effectively taken the electrons rather than shared them, which is an ionic bond.

## Dipole moments

A positive-to-negative partial charge in an atom is measured as its **dipole moment**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Bond polarity** | A measure of how equally or unequally the electrons in any covalent bond are shared |
| **Polar covalent bond** | A bond in which one of the atoms exerts a greater attraction for the bonding electrons than the other |
| **Polarity** | A separation of positive and negative charge |
| **Nonpolar bond** | A bond in which the bonding electrons are shared equally |
| **Dipole moment** | The measure of a positive-to-negative partial charge in an atom |

# 8.5 Drawing Lewis Structures

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Starting the structure

**Step 1: calculate the total valence electrons.** Everything that follows is an exercise in distributing that fixed total, so getting the count wrong at the start makes the rest of the work worthless no matter how careful it is.

## Formal charge

Once a structure is drawn, **formal charge** tells you whether it is a good one:

$$\text{Formal charge} = \text{valence } e^- - \left( \frac{\text{bonding } e^-}{2} + \text{nonbonding } e^- \right)$$

Bonding electrons are halved because they are shared between two atoms; nonbonding electrons belong entirely to the atom that carries them, so they count in full.

### Choosing the best structure

Two rules select between competing structures:

- **Minimise the charges.**
- **Place negative charges on the electronegative atoms.**

The second follows from what electronegativity means: an electronegative atom is the one that attracts electrons, so it is the one that can carry extra negative charge most comfortably.

## Examples

**$\mathrm{CO_2}$** is drawn as $\mathrm{O=C=O}$. The formal charges are $\mathrm{C} = 0$ and $\mathrm{O} = 0$ throughout — every atom carries zero, which is as close to the "minimise the charges" ideal as a structure can get.

**$\mathrm{NO_3^-}$** is drawn as $\mathrm{O=N-O^-}$, and it has a resonance structure with the double bond shifting position. That behaviour is the subject of the next section.

## Practice

Draw Lewis structures for:

- $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$
- $\mathrm{HCN}$
- $\mathrm{ClO_2^-}$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Formal charge** | Valence electrons minus the sum of half the bonding electrons and all the nonbonding electrons |

# 8.6 Resonance Structures and Exceptions to the Octet Rule

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Two sections here, and both are about the same admission: a single Lewis structure obeying the octet rule does not always describe a real molecule.

## Resonance structures

**Resonance structures** are multiple valid Lewis structures for a molecule or ion, arising from delocalised electrons.

### Ozone, $\mathrm{O_3}$

$$\mathrm{O=O-O} \leftrightarrow \mathrm{O-O=O}$$

The measurement that settles the matter: **both $\mathrm{O-O}$ bonds are $1.28\ \text{Å}$** — shorter than a single bond but longer than a double bond. Neither drawn structure is what the molecule actually is. The real molecule is a single thing in which the electrons are spread over both bonds, so both bonds come out intermediate in length.

### Carbonate, $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$

The carbonate ion is drawn with one double bond and two single $\mathrm{O^-}$ bonds, and there are two other resonance forms in which the double bond shifts to a different oxygen.

### Practice

Identify resonance structures for $\mathrm{SO_2}$ and $\mathrm{NO_2^-}$.

## Exceptions to the octet rule

There are three kinds.

### 1. Odd number of electrons

Molecules with unpaired electrons cannot have every atom at eight, because eight is even and the total available is not.

Examples: $\mathrm{NO}$, $\mathrm{ClO_2}$.

For $\mathrm{NO}$: $\mathrm{N}$ has 5 valence electrons and $\mathrm{O}$ has 6, giving a total of 11 — an odd number, so at least one electron must be left unpaired.

### 2. Fewer than 8 electrons (incomplete octet)

Elements like $\mathrm{B}$ and $\mathrm{Be}$ may form compounds with fewer than 8 electrons.

Example: in $\mathrm{BF_3}$, boron has 6 electrons from its three single bonds to fluorine.

### 3. Expanded octet

Elements in Period 3 and beyond — such as $\mathrm{P}$, $\mathrm{S}$ and $\mathrm{Cl}$ — can use d orbitals to hold more than 8 electrons. The period restriction is the key: Period 2 elements have no d orbitals available, which is why this exception never applies to them.

Example: in $\mathrm{PCl_5}$, phosphorus has 10 electrons from its five single bonds to chlorine.

### Practice

Classify the exceptions to the octet rule in $\mathrm{XeF_4}$, $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ and $\mathrm{NO}$.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Resonance structures** | Multiple valid Lewis structures for a molecule or ion, due to delocalised electrons |
| **Incomplete octet** | An exception in which elements such as $\mathrm{B}$ and $\mathrm{Be}$ form compounds with fewer than 8 electrons |
| **Expanded octet** | An exception in which elements in Period 3 and beyond use d orbitals to hold more than 8 electrons |

# 9.1 Naming Binary Molecular Compounds

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What they are

**Binary molecular compounds** are formed by nonmetal + nonmetal combinations — $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2O}$, $\mathrm{NH_3}$.

Unlike ionic compounds, they consist of **discrete molecules**, not formula units. That difference is what makes the naming system different: an ionic formula only states a ratio, so it needs no count, whereas a molecular formula states how many atoms are actually in the molecule, and the name has to say so.

## Naming rules

### Order of elements

1. Name the first element in the formula as the element name.
2. Name the second element using the root of the element name plus the suffix **-ide**, as with the anions of ionic compounds.

### Prefixes for atom count

Use prefixes to indicate the number of atoms of each element.

**Omit the prefix "mono-" for the first element if only one atom is present.** So $\mathrm{CO}$ is carbon monoxide, not "monocarbon monoxide".

The guide gives a table of prefixes to memorise, with the tip: **only memorise the table one day before the test.**

## From formula to name

1. Identify the elements in the formula. For $\mathrm{NF_3}$, these are nitrogen and fluorine.
2. Assign prefixes based on the number of atoms. Here $\mathrm{N} = 1$, so no prefix is used, since it is the first element.

## Common mistakes to avoid

**Confusing molecular with ionic compounds.** Molecular compounds never contain metal ions. $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ is ionic, not molecular; $\mathrm{PCl_3}$ is molecular. Checking whether a metal is present is the first thing to do, because it decides which naming system applies at all — and prefixes belong only to the molecular one.

**Incorrect prefix placement.** Always apply prefixes to both elements, except for "mono-" on the first element. So $\mathrm{N_2O}$ is dinitrogen monoxide, not "nitrogen monoxide".

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Binary molecular compound** | A compound formed by nonmetal + nonmetal combinations, consisting of discrete molecules rather than formula units |

# 9.2 Metallic Bonding and the Properties of Metals

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The atomic structure of metals

A metal has two key components:

- **Cations** — positively charged metal ions formed by losing valence electrons, such as $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$.
- The **electron sea** — delocalised valence electrons freely moving throughout the metal lattice.

The model analogy: think of the metal cations as islands submerged in a sea of electrons that hold them together.

## Physical properties explained by metallic bonding

Every property in the table is the electron sea doing something. Learn the explanations rather than the list — the questions ask why.

| Property | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **Metallic lustre** | Free electrons absorb and re-emit light across the visible spectrum |
| **Conductivity** | Mobile electrons carry electric current (charge) and thermal energy (vibrations) |
| **Malleability** | Applying force causes cations to slide, but the electron sea prevents repulsion and breaking |
| **Ductility** | Cations can be drawn into wires without breaking bonds, supported by the electron sea |
| **High density** | Close-packed crystal structures, such as face-centred cubic, in most metals |

Malleability and ductility are the same mechanism seen twice: because the electrons are not tied to particular cations, moving the cations past each other never brings like charges face to face, so the metal deforms instead of shattering.

## The strength of metallic bonding

Two factors control it.

**1. Ionic radius.** A smaller radius means a stronger attraction to the electron sea. The radii increase in the order $\mathrm{Li^+} < \mathrm{Na^+} < \mathrm{K^+}$, so lithium's bonding is the strongest of the three.

**2. Number of valence electrons.** More electrons means stronger bonding: $\mathrm{Na}$ (1 e⁻) $<$ $\mathrm{Mg}$ (2 e⁻) $<$ $\mathrm{Al}$ (3 e⁻). More valence electrons donated means a denser electron sea holding the cations together.

### Worked question

**Why is magnesium's melting point ($650\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$) higher than sodium's ($98\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$)?**

$\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ has a smaller radius and more valence electrons (2 e⁻ against sodium's 1 e⁻), leading to stronger metallic bonding. Both factors point the same way, which is why the difference in melting point is so large.

## Metallic against ionic bonds

| Feature | Metallic bond | Ionic bond |
|---|---|---|
| Bonding particles | Cations + electron sea | Cations + anions (electrostatic attraction) |
| Electron movement | Delocalised (free to move) | Localised (fixed in lattice) |
| Conductivity (solid) | High (electrons mobile) | Low (ions fixed in place) |
| Mechanical behaviour | Malleable/ductile (flexible) | Brittle (shatters under force) |
| Examples | $\mathrm{Fe}$, $\mathrm{Cu}$, $\mathrm{Al}$ | $\mathrm{NaCl}$, $\mathrm{MgO}$ |

The last three rows all descend from the first. Whether the electrons can move decides whether the solid conducts, and whether the charged particles can slide past each other decides whether it bends or shatters.

## Alloys

**Alloys** are mixtures of metals — steel is $\mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{C}$. They enhance strength by disrupting the packing of the cations.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Electron sea** | Delocalised valence electrons freely moving throughout the metal lattice |
| **Metallic lustre** | The shine of a metal, caused by free electrons absorbing and re-emitting light across the visible spectrum |
| **Malleability** | The ability to deform under force as cations slide, with the electron sea preventing repulsion and breaking |
| **Ductility** | The ability to be drawn into wires without breaking bonds, supported by the electron sea |
| **Alloy** | A mixture of metals, such as steel ($\mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{C}$), which enhances strength by disrupting cation packing |

# 9.3 Molecular Geometry: VSEPR Theory and Applications

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The core principle

The aim of **VSEPR theory** is to predict three-dimensional molecular shapes by minimising repulsion between **electron domains**, both bonding and nonbonding.

Three rules govern it:

1. **Lone pair repulsion.** Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs. Water's bent shape is the result of its 2 lone pairs.
2. **Double and triple bonds count as 1 electron domain.** $\mathrm{CO_2}$ has two double bonds, which is 2 domains, so the molecule is linear.
3. **Bond angle trends.** Lone pairs compress bond angles. Compare $\mathrm{NH_3}$ at $107°$ with $\mathrm{CH_4}$ at $109.5°$: both have four domains, but the lone pair in ammonia pushes the bonding pairs closer together.

Rule 2 is the one most often forgotten. A domain is a region of electron density, not a count of bonds, so a double bond occupies one region just as a single bond does.

## Step-by-step shape prediction

1. **Draw the Lewis structure.** Identify the central atom and count the valence electrons.
2. **Count electron domains.** Bonding domains equal the number of bonds, with single, double and triple bonds each counting as 1 domain. Add the lone pairs.
3. **Determine the electron domain geometry.** 2 domains give linear, 3 give trigonal planar, 4 give tetrahedral, and so on.
4. **Predict the molecular shape.** Ignore the lone pairs for the final shape — for example, 4 domains with 1 lone pair gives trigonal pyramidal.

Step 4 is where the two geometries part company. The lone pairs are still there and still repelling, which is why they set the domain geometry and squeeze the angles, but they are invisible when you name the shape because a shape is described by where the atoms are.

## Electron domains and shapes

| Domains | Domain geometry | Bonding domains | Nonbonding domains | Molecular shape | Bond angle | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | Linear | 2 | 0 | Linear | $180°$ | $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{HCN}$ |
| 3 | Trigonal planar | 3 | 0 | Trigonal planar | $120°$ | $\mathrm{BF_3}$, $\mathrm{SO_3}$ |
| 3 | Trigonal planar | 2 | 1 | Bent (V-shaped) | $\sim 117°$ | $\mathrm{SO_2}$, $\mathrm{NO_2^-}$ |
| 4 | Tetrahedral | 4 | 0 | Tetrahedral | $109.5°$ | $\mathrm{CH_4}$, $\mathrm{CCl_4}$ |
| 4 | Tetrahedral | 3 | 1 | Trigonal pyramidal | $107°$ | $\mathrm{NH_3}$, $\mathrm{PCl_3}$ |
| 4 | Tetrahedral | 2 | 2 | Bent | $104.5°$ | $\mathrm{H_2O}$, $\mathrm{SCl_2}$ |
| 5 | Trigonal bipyramidal | 5 | 0 | Trigonal bipyramidal | $90°/120°$ | $\mathrm{PF_5}$, $\mathrm{PCl_5}$ |
| 5 | Trigonal bipyramidal | 4 | 1 | Seesaw | $\sim 90°/120°$ | $\mathrm{SF_4}$, $\mathrm{TeCl_4}$ |
| 5 | Trigonal bipyramidal | 3 | 2 | T-shaped | $\sim 90°$ | $\mathrm{ClF_3}$, $\mathrm{BrF_3}$ |
| 5 | Trigonal bipyramidal | 2 | 3 | Linear | $180°$ | $\mathrm{XeF_2}$, $\mathrm{I_3^-}$ |
| 6 | Octahedral | 6 | 0 | Octahedral | $90°$ | $\mathrm{SF_6}$, $\mathrm{MoF_6}$ |
| 6 | Octahedral | 5 | 1 | Square pyramidal | $\sim 90°$ | $\mathrm{BrF_5}$, $\mathrm{IF_5}$ |
| 6 | Octahedral | 4 | 2 | Square planar | $90°$ | $\mathrm{XeF_4}$, $\mathrm{PtCl_4^{2-}}$ |

Reading down the four-domain block shows the pattern in miniature: the domain geometry stays tetrahedral throughout while the shape changes from tetrahedral to trigonal pyramidal to bent, and the bond angle falls from $109.5°$ to $107°$ to $104.5°$ as each lone pair is added.

## Molecular polarity

**Nonpolar molecules:**

1. Symmetrical shape — linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral and so on.
2. All surrounding atoms identical, as in $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{CCl_4}$ and $\mathrm{BF_3}$.

**Polar molecules:**

1. Asymmetrical shape — bent, trigonal pyramidal, seesaw and so on.
2. Surrounding atoms differ in electronegativity, as in $\mathrm{H_2O}$, $\mathrm{NH_3}$ and $\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}$.

$\mathrm{CH_4}$ is nonpolar: it is tetrahedral, and all the surrounding atoms are hydrogen. A symmetrical arrangement of identical bonds means the individual bond dipoles have nothing to add up to.

## Practice problems

**Predict the shape of $\mathrm{SO_3^{2-}}$.**

- Lewis structure: $\mathrm{S}$ is central, with $6 + 3 \times 6 + 2 = 26$ electrons; $\mathrm{S}$ has 1 lone pair and 3 bonding pairs.
- Electron domains: 4, being 3 bonding plus 1 nonbonding, so the domain geometry is tetrahedral.
- From the table, 4 domains with 3 bonding and 1 nonbonding gives a **trigonal pyramidal** shape.

**A polarity example.** A square planar molecule with identical $\mathrm{F}$ atoms is symmetrical, so it is nonpolar.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **VSEPR theory** | A theory that predicts three-dimensional molecular shapes by minimising repulsion between electron domains, both bonding and nonbonding |
| **Electron domain** | A region of electron density around the central atom; a single, double or triple bond each counts as 1 domain, as does each lone pair |
| **Electron domain geometry** | The arrangement set by the total number of domains: 2 linear, 3 trigonal planar, 4 tetrahedral, and so on |
| **Molecular shape** | The arrangement obtained by ignoring the lone pairs in the domain geometry |
| **Nonpolar molecule** | A molecule with a symmetrical shape and identical surrounding atoms |
| **Polar molecule** | A molecule with an asymmetrical shape whose surrounding atoms differ in electronegativity |

# 9.4 Hybridisation and Bonding Theories

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

VSEPR predicts the shape. Hybridisation explains how the central atom's orbitals arrange themselves to produce it.

## Hybrid orbitals

**Hybridisation** is the mixing of atomic orbitals (s, p, d) to form new hybrid orbitals with equal energy and specific geometries.

| Hybridisation | Atomic orbitals mixed | Electron domains | Geometry | Bond angle | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $sp$ | 1 s + 1 p | 2 | Linear | $180°$ | $\mathrm{BeF_2}$, $\mathrm{C_2H_2}$ (acetylene) |
| $sp^2$ | 1 s + 2 p | 3 | Trigonal planar | $120°$ | $\mathrm{BF_3}$, $\mathrm{C_2H_4}$ (ethylene) |
| $sp^3$ | 1 s + 3 p | 4 | Tetrahedral | $109.5°$ | $\mathrm{CH_4}$, $\mathrm{NH_3}$, $\mathrm{H_2O}$ |
| $sp^3d$ | 1 s + 3 p + 1 d | 5 | Trigonal bipyramidal | $90°/120°$ | $\mathrm{PF_5}$, $\mathrm{SF_4}$, $\mathrm{BrF_3}$ |
| $sp^3d^2$ | 1 s + 3 p + 2 d | 6 | Octahedral | $90°$ | $\mathrm{SF_6}$, $\mathrm{XeF_4}$, $\mathrm{IF_5}$ |

**The shortcut: electron domains = number of hybrid orbitals.** So 5 domains means $sp^3d$. The superscripts in each label are just a count of how many orbitals went into the mix, and that count must equal the number of domains coming out — which is why the table can be reconstructed rather than memorised.

## Sigma and pi bonds

| Bond type | Formation | Strength | Rotation | Occurrence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\sigma$ (sigma) | Head-on overlap of orbitals (s-s, s-p, p-p) | Strongest | Free | All single bonds; 1 per multiple bond |
| $\pi$ (pi) | Side-by-side overlap of parallel p orbitals | Weaker than $\sigma$ | Restricted | Double bonds (1 $\pi$), triple bonds (2 $\pi$) |

The rotation column is the practically useful one. A $\sigma$ bond's head-on overlap is unchanged when one end turns, so rotation is free; a $\pi$ bond's side-by-side overlap is destroyed by rotation, so double and triple bonds are locked rigid.

### Examples

**$\mathrm{C_2H_4}$ (ethylene):** the $\mathrm{C=C}$ double bond is 1 $\sigma$ from $sp^2$-$sp^2$ overlap plus 1 $\pi$ from p-p side overlap.

**$\mathrm{C_2H_2}$ (acetylene):** the $\mathrm{C \equiv C}$ triple bond is 1 $\sigma$ from $sp$-$sp$ overlap plus 2 $\pi$ from p-p side overlaps.

## Delocalisation and resonance

**Resonance structures** are multiple valid Lewis structures for a molecule, as in $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$ and $\mathrm{O_3}$.

$\mathrm{NO_3^-}$ has 3 resonance structures, and its $\pi$ electrons are delocalised over the $\mathrm{N-O}$ bonds. Delocalisation is the reason the several drawn structures are needed: the $\pi$ electrons are not confined to one bond, so no single structure can place them correctly.

## Practice problems

**What is the hybridisation of the central atom in $\mathrm{CO_2}$?**

Linear geometry gives 2 electron domains, so the hybridisation is $sp$.

**And for a tetrahedral molecule?**

A tetrahedral shape gives 4 electron domains, so the hybridisation is $sp^3$.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Hybridisation** | The mixing of atomic orbitals (s, p, d) to form new hybrid orbitals with equal energy and specific geometries |
| **Sigma ($\sigma$) bond** | A bond formed by head-on overlap of orbitals; the strongest bond type, with free rotation, found in all single bonds and once per multiple bond |
| **Pi ($\pi$) bond** | A bond formed by side-by-side overlap of parallel p orbitals; weaker than a sigma bond, with restricted rotation, found in double bonds (1) and triple bonds (2) |
| **Resonance structures** | Multiple valid Lewis structures for a molecule, arising because the $\pi$ electrons are delocalised |

# 9.5 Intermolecular and Intramolecular Forces

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The distinction

**Intramolecular forces** are the forces that exist inside molecules — only the covalent bond.

**Intermolecular forces** are the forces of attraction between neighbouring molecules.

The two prefixes are the whole distinction: *intra* is within one molecule, *inter* is between separate molecules. Breaking an intramolecular force means destroying the molecule; overcoming an intermolecular force only means separating molecules from one another.

## The three intermolecular forces

### London dispersion forces

A force of attraction between **induced dipoles**, present in **all molecular substances**.

Because they are induced rather than permanent, nothing about a molecule's structure is required for them to exist — which is why this is the one force every molecular substance has.

### Dipole-dipole forces

Attractions between the opposite charges of neighbouring dipoles.

Polar molecules have **permanent dipoles**. Whether a molecule is a permanent dipole depends on two things: whether it has polar bonds, and the geometry of the molecule. Both conditions are needed — polar bonds arranged symmetrically cancel out, which is why molecular shape has to be settled before polarity can be decided.

### Hydrogen bonding

The extremely strong dipole-dipole force between the $\mathrm{H}$ atom of one molecule and the $\mathrm{N}$, $\mathrm{O}$ or $\mathrm{F}$ atoms of another molecule.

Hydrogen bonding is a special case of the dipole-dipole force rather than a separate mechanism, distinguished by how strong it is and by the restriction to those three partner atoms.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Intramolecular forces** | The forces that exist inside molecules (only the covalent bond) |
| **Intermolecular forces** | The forces of attraction between neighbouring molecules |
| **London dispersion forces** | A force of attraction between induced dipoles, present in all molecular substances |
| **Dipole-dipole forces** | Attractions between opposite charges of neighbouring dipoles |
| **Permanent dipole** | A polar molecule; whether a molecule is one depends on whether it has polar bonds and on the geometry of the molecule |
| **Hydrogen bonding** | The extremely strong dipole-dipole force between the $\mathrm{H}$ atom of one molecule and the $\mathrm{N}$, $\mathrm{O}$ or $\mathrm{F}$ atoms of another |
